newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Tarkett says merger plans on track.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Tarkett says merger plans on track.

text.p: German floor covering manufacturer Tarkett AG on Thursday said it was on track to merge with Sommer Allibert of France this year despite attempts to block the fusion.
"We are right on track," chief executive Lars Wisen told Reuters in a television interview.
Wisen told a news conference he expected cartel authorities in Germany and the U.S. to approve the link-up over the coming weeks, and said the merger should go ahead in mid-November.

Tarkett plans to merge its floor covering business with Sommer Allibert to create Tarkett-Sommer AG, one of the world leaders in this segment with annual sales of 2.6 billion marks, 27 plants worldwide and 8,800 employees.
Rival American firm Armstrong World Industries, had sought to block the merger deal but Wisen said current indications were that this was unlikely to succeed.
The Ontario Securities Commission, to which Armstrong had appealed, this week decided not to intervene in the Tarkett-Sommer plans, Lisen noted.
The German firm also said it was heading for higher earnings this year after reporting net profit of 27.9 million marks in the first half, marginally up from 27.7 million.
Group sales advanced 13.2 percent to 753.6 million marks from 666 million marks in the period.
Tarkett noted that its profits had improved substantially in the second quarter, when net earnings rose 23.6 percent to 17.3 million marks.
"We believe 1997 will be a better year than 1996," Wisen said. "We should see a nice development in the second half."
Tarkett is aiming to reapproach 1995 profit levels, when it posted a record operating result of 146.2 million marks. In 1996, operating profits were 136.3 million.

The merger deal, announced in May, involves Sommer-Allibert taking a 60 percent stake in Tarkett in a deal valuing Tarkett shares at 32.75 marks, which in return will pay 705 million marks in cash for Sommer's floor covering business.
Tarkett has been put on credit watch by several rating agencies as a result of the deal, which it plans to finance using debt.
But Wisen said he was unperturbed by this move.
"It is normal that we would be put on credit-watch after such a deal. The important thing is that analysts seem happy with it," he said.

Wisen said he expected the German Cartel Office to rule on the merger project before the end of August. A ruling from U.S. authorities would follow in September and the motion would be put to shareholders the following month.
